items.content:
RT @MsftSecIntel: Microsoft’s FORGE Lab identified several memory-safety issues in Rust's core and std libraries, including cases where code written entirely in safe Rust can trigger undefined behavior. https://t.co/2iVeFfAb0H 

The research examines three recurring patterns of misplaced trust in unsafe code: trusting code not to panic, trusting user-provided implementations to be correct, and trusting the underlying system. Findings include issues affecting iterator cloning, string replacement, and interactions with the operating system.

Using Hyenas, FORGE's research version of codename MDASH, researchers combined AI-assisted vulnerability discovery with technical investigation and validation. They investigated the underlying code, reproduced the bugs, assessed potential security impact, and worked with Rust maintainers to report and fix them.

While Rust's ownership model and type system prevent entire classes of memory-safety vulnerabilities, unsafe implementations underneath safe APIs must still uphold those guarantees. The findings illustrate how subtle mistakes in foundational libraries can lead to undefined behavior, and why Rust's safety model remains important even when bugs are discovered.

Read the analysis for details on the findings, root causes, upstream fixes, and lessons for developers working with unsafe Rust.

items.content:
Remember: the codebase you're reviewing is alive, and it won't stop changing just because you're taking notes.

When documenting a potential vulnerability, don't record only the filename and line number. Code moves, code changes, files get renamed, and your reference might point to something completely different by the time someone reads your findings.

Always keep the filename, line number, commit hash, and a copy of the relevant code, along with an explanation of the issue. If you include a link, make sure it points to that specific commit, not to the branch.

Your notes should still make sense after the code has changed.

​

Based on the telemetry reviewed, the campaign has been active since at least early October. Initially, the malicious Lambda functions were predominantly hosted in the 𝗔𝗪𝗦 𝗨𝗦 𝗘𝗮𝘀𝘁 (𝗡. The threat actors use AWS Lambda Function URLs as the initial landing page, often masquerading as Microsoft 365 services such as 𝗢𝗻𝗲𝗗𝗿𝗶𝘃𝗲. Victims are presented with a pop-up message which, when clicked, redirects them through a series of security-check pages before ultimately landing on a fraudulent Microsoft sign-in page utilizing an 𝗔𝗱𝘃𝗲𝗿𝘀𝗮𝗿𝘆-𝗶𝗻-𝘁𝗵𝗲-𝗠𝗶𝗱𝗱𝗹𝗲 (𝗔𝗶𝗧𝗠) phishing framework.

​
Defenders should review inbound email traffic for URLs matching the following pattern:
​
https://{32-character-identifier}.lambda-url.{aws-region}.on.aws/?{tracking-parameter}=*@*
​
A high-fidelity detection can be achieved by combining this URL pattern with:
​
IsFirstContact == true

What I am saying is *with tools* -- e.g. with the headless API for the best commercial decompilers, and emulation/virtualization solutions (like Corellium Falcon), etc -- which in total, cost hundreds of thousands of dollars, and with a large sample size of working production grade exploits to take inspiration from, the best open source models are *still* completely incapable of autonomously designing and building production grade exploits/exploit chains against the major mobile attack surfaces. With the very close and careful guidance of an expert exploit developer with years of experience, they can be halfway useful. 

They can find bugs, sure. But that is infinitely easier than the work involved with curating, exploiting for full effect (i.e. RCE, SBX Escape or LPE) and chaining. 

However, the very best closed models, in their various cyber-vetted versions, are capable of doing so. This only became the case in the last 6 weeks or so.

Exploit development is doable with open-weights but it does incur a decent amount of overhead. If you aren’t familiar with a specific subsystem or interactions between components then you may have a rough time. With the open weights, I was able to discover 4 within a more hardened surface (oob write, cross-priv info leak, 2x null-deref DoS). With a library of primitives, K3 or GLM5.3 can do well.

Daybreak is excellent though, I would highly recommend it for VR; but I was able to net these 4 reportable bugs in <72 hours with an open-weight setup — so we shouldn’t throw shade at open-weights, they’re pretty great when focused.

items.content:
RT @MalwareTechBlog: I love that people want to assume that I formed my opinions on the viability of current generation open-weight LLMs for enabling low-skilled criminals to find useful zero-day exploits, based on having just never used an LLM at all. 

The first thing I did when Anthropic added me to their CVP was build an autonomous zero-day exploitation pipeline. I've since backported it to use open-weight models because the token cost was insane, so I have a fairly good feel for both current frontier and open-weight model capabilities.

I'm well aware of what LLMs are capable of doing, and that they can, with the right steering or harness find zero-day exploits. Where we drift off course is with the claim that low-skilled criminals can just pick up something like GLM and find viable zero-day exploits.

I think that: 

a) More than 90% of CVEs are functionally useless for threat actors. Threat actors have a very specific operational needs and "random issue in random software" does not fall into their scope. 

b) Many (quite possibly even the majority of) critical rated CVEs are not exploitable under real-world conditions in a way that is useful to threat actors. There's entire teams in China dedicated to n-day exploitation and watching them will give you a good feel for what percent of critical RCEs are actually useful.

c) Threat actor with no exploit development background and minimal technical skills, even with access to a completely unrestricted open-weight LLMs, would struggle or completely fail to find useful zero-day exploits.

d) People with very little experience in software exploitation, Large Language Models, and CTI, are watching professional vulnerability researchers working with next-gen frontier models and ending up with a wildly unrealistic beliefs of just how "easy" what they are doing is.

e) There is an extremely noticeable lack of both zero-day exploitation and use of novel (non-public) n-day exploits by all threat actors, especially unskilled ones, and proponents of the "anyone can just pick up GLM and find useful zero-day exploits" theory continually refuse to even acknowledge that fact, let alone attempt to explain it.

I'm not coming at this from the position of some dude who just logs on to social media to says uninformed shit. I'm coming at this from the perspective of a researcher who has spent thousands of hours since LLMs came out researching their capabilities, and has also spent their entire career tracking threat actors and their capabilities. 

I have a mountain of real-world data, because the low-skilled AI-powered threat actors have a high tendency to accidentally infect themselves with their own malware. This often results in them exfiltrate their entire hard disk, along with all their AI prompt logs, to a vibe-coded C2 with client-side authentication (the admin credentials are hardcoded into the javascript or something equally stupid, so anyone can log in and download it).

My entire career I've been very pro "degrees and certs don't matter, everyone is welcome, and the best way to gain experience is hands-on practical work". But when I have some dude whose only experience is essentially just "downloaded abliterated GLM and scared himself with it", I feel like it's necessary to draw a line somewhere.

It's not just the bad opinions, everyone has bad opinions on something, I have plenty. It's that resources are actively being diverted away from addressing real and pressing issues in cybersecurity, as a result of FUD being spread about imaginary GLM-powered zero-day wielding scriptkiddies.

items.content:
In my own head, I have a sort of visual-spacial representation how how the various system internals of iOS work 

Many other vulnerability researchers have said that their minds work similarly to reason about systems

So what I did was try to create 3D representations to map functions across all the different software/firmware/hardware layers of abstraction that these subsystems work (in this case, iOS 27's SPTM). One of the 3D representations even presents an immersive 'video game' of sorts, which lets the agents "walk through" the system 

I have found this to be a helpful resource for agents, keeping them more tightly grounded to the functionality of these complex systems, though I don't have formal benchmarks (which are overrated anyway)
